A Bronze Age civilisation on the island of Crete, from about 2700 to 1450 BCE, often called the first civilisation in Europe. It is known for great palaces, the largest at Knossos, and for bright wall paintings of bulls, dolphins and processions.

The name is modern. The archaeologist Arthur Evans, who dug Knossos from 1900, named it after Minos, the king of Greek legend who kept the Minotaur in a labyrinth. What the Minoans called themselves is unknown.

What we know of them:

  • From around 1900 BCE they built large palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, with storerooms, courtyards, light wells and drains. They had no strong defensive walls.
  • They were traders and seafarers. They sent oil, wine and fine crafts across the Aegean and to Egypt and the Levant, and brought back copper and tin.
  • They wrote in Linear A, a script still not deciphered, so their language is unknown.
  • Their art shows bull-leaping, where young people somersaulted over charging bulls.

Their culture spread across the Aegean islands, including Thera. The eruption of Thera, around 1600 BCE, buried the town of Akrotiri under ash and may have hit Crete with tsunamis, but the palaces went on for generations.

Around 1450 BCE most palaces were destroyed. Afterwards Knossos was run by Greek-speakers from the mainland, the Mycenaeans, who adapted Linear A into Linear B to write Greek. Minoan art and ways lived on in Mycenaean culture, and memories of Crete survived in Greek myth.
